claims.text: Inhibiting the mobility of reduced noble-metal species during nucleation favors formation of single-phase homogeneous high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles over phase-separated or segregated products.
Alloy formation under mobility-restricted conditions proceeds through stochastic, frozen-in incorporation of metal atoms.
The starting material is a homogeneously mixed system containing five or more noble-metal single-source precursors.
Lowering the reaction temperature can restrict the mobility of reducing and nucleating metal species.
Increasing solvent viscosity can restrict the mobility of reducing and nucleating metal species.
Surface-anchoring ligands can restrict the mobility of reducing and nucleating metal species.
Low-temperature reduction with controlled cooling limits atomic diffusion during nucleation.
Restricted atomic diffusion freezes randomly distributed atoms into the growing nanoparticle.
Under kinetic restriction, reduced metal atoms are captured by nucleating seeds before they can diffuse and segregate.
Greater atomic mobility permits element-specific aggregation and phase separation despite staggered precursor-reduction events.
The mobility-inhibited synthesis will yield a single-phase homogeneous alloy with a uniform elemental distribution relative to the unchanged high-mobility baseline.
The mobility-inhibited synthesis will preserve high surface-atom exposure suitable for catalytic applications.
Typical conditions that do not specifically restrict atomic mobility often produce phase separation or elemental segregation.
Typical conditions that do not specifically restrict atomic mobility often produce uncontrolled nanoparticle morphology.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily to low-temperature reduction of homogeneous, single-source multimetal precursors for which kinetic control is feasible.
The mechanism may not apply to high-temperature or melt-phase synthesis because atomic mobility and diffusion are unrestricted.
Failure of mobility-inhibited synthesis to improve homogeneous single-phase alloying significantly relative to an otherwise identical control would falsify the hypothesis.
